name: Snipe
question: Why is it accelerating now?
intro: Read changes in demand before the move becomes obvious: buyers, size, selling, absorption, and attention.

lessons.title: Price moves at the margin
lessons.question: Did capital grow, or did the last price change?
lessons.definition: The next trade changes the price available to the trade after it. In an AMM pool, reserves and liquidity shape that price.
lessons.why: A small trade can change the displayed valuation of the whole supply.
checks: Exact pool and current liquidity
Trade size relative to pool depth
Market cap change versus observed trade value
lessons.healthy: Price changes are read alongside pool depth and surrounding trades.
lessons.dangerous: A market-cap jump is treated as the same amount of new capital.
lessons.takeaway: A new price can revalue the whole supply.
example: A token has 1 million circulating units at $0.10.
The displayed price rises to $0.12: market cap rises from $100k to $120k.
That $20k change does not tell you how much was traded.
evidence: Choose an exact contract. Compare estimated MC tiers with observed swap value; these are different measures.
lessons.deeper: The original outline uses an auction analogy. Many meme pools use automated pricing instead of an order book. The useful shared idea is marginal pricing, not a literal match between named buyers and sellers.

lessons.title: Liquidity & price impact
lessons.question: How much does this order disturb the pool?
lessons.definition: Price impact is the change in execution price caused by your order relative to available liquidity.
lessons.why: The same dollar order can produce very different fills in different pools.
checks: Current executable quote for the intended size
Pool depth and route
Impact, fees, and slippage tolerance separately
lessons.healthy: The order fits the quote and the expected cost is understood.
lessons.dangerous: Thin depth or broad tolerance turns a modest order into a poor fill.
lessons.mistake: Expecting equal buy sizes to create equal moves.
example: Compare a $1k order in a deep pool and a thin pool.
The thin pool may offer a much worse average execution price.
Compare the actual quotes, not just the chart prices.
evidence: Check reported liquidity as context. Obtain current impact and execution quotes externally.
lessons.deeper: Price sensitivity is not automatically strength: it can amplify selling too. A ratio of price change to sampled net buying is descriptive, not a stable capital-efficiency score. Liquidity, routes, and missing trades can all change the comparison.

lessons.title: Buy/sell pressure
lessons.question: Are the buys actually outweighing the sells?
lessons.definition: Pressure combines trade value, frequency, and how long the activity persists.
lessons.why: Many small buys can be outweighed by one large sell.
checks: Buy and sell value in the same window
Typical sizes and the largest trades
Whether the pattern persists in the next window
lessons.healthy: Buying persists and repeated selling meets new demand.
lessons.dangerous: Green transaction counts hide large sell value.
lessons.mistake: Counting colors instead of measuring value.
lessons.takeaway: Read size, frequency, and persistence together.
example: 20 buys × $100 = $2,000 bought.
This sample has 19 more buys, but $3,000 more sell value.
evidence: Compare buy/sell value and swap sizes for one listing and time window. Net value describes the returned sample.
lessons.deeper: Size × frequency × persistence is a thinking aid, not a defined trading score. Observed buy value minus sell value is not a measurement of total capital entering the token, and it does not by itself determine the price outcome.

lessons.title: Supply transfer
lessons.question: Whose inventory is changing hands?
lessons.definition: Supply transfer moves inventory from early holders to later buyers.
lessons.why: Remaining low-cost inventory can become future sell pressure.
checks: Early-wallet balances before and after sales
Transfers versus executed sells
Remaining inventory relative to liquidity
lessons.healthy: Actual sales and new ownership can be traced.
lessons.dangerous: Transfers to related wallets disguise continuing control.
lessons.mistake: Assuming lower concentration proves independent ownership.
lessons.takeaway: Track what remains, not just what moved.
example: An early wallet holds 8% of supply.
It transfers 5% to fresh addresses and still holds 3%.
The visible balance fell; common control may not have changed.
lessons.external: Use an explorer and wallet history to trace transfers, trades, and related balances. Meme Fast does not establish common ownership.
lessons.deeper: Sellable supply is a hypothesis about inventory that may be offered, not an observable list of everyone willing to sell. Holder turnover needs transaction history; a snapshot alone cannot establish it.

lessons.title: Early wallet flow
lessons.question: Who is behind the buying?
lessons.definition: Wallet flow asks whether a participant is buying, holding, transferring, or selling over time.
lessons.why: The same trade value can come from independent buyers or one coordinated operator.
checks: Wallet history and remaining exposure
Funding links and transfers
Observed entry cost and prior sales
lessons.healthy: Attribution and behavior are supported by traceable history.
lessons.dangerous: A reputation label or many addresses substitutes for evidence.
lessons.mistake: Treating every buy as equally informative.
lessons.takeaway: Investigate the source of the flow.
example: Ten addresses each buy $500.
All ten were funded through the same small wallet moments earlier.
That is a coordination lead, not ten proven independent buyers.
evidence: Use transaction senders as leads, then trace them externally. Routers can appear as senders; wallet identity and cost basis are not verified here.
lessons.deeper: A transaction bundle groups transactions; a wallet cluster is an inference about related addresses. Neither automatically proves malicious intent. Shared exchange funding, routers, and incomplete trade history can mislead attribution.

lessons.title: Demand acceleration
lessons.question: Is the activity strengthening or just staying busy?
lessons.definition: Acceleration is a change in the rate of activity. It asks whether demand is strengthening across comparable observations.
lessons.why: A busy token can be slowing down while its chart still looks strong.
checks: Equal, separate bars: price response, buy value, sizes, and frequency
New buyers and holder growth, with identity and coverage checked
Sell-size contraction, absorption, and credible attention growth
lessons.healthy: Several comparable observations support stronger demand and responsive price.
lessons.dangerous: Bots, larger window totals, or one candle create apparent acceleration.
lessons.mistake: Waiting for a giant candle, then assuming the engine is still strengthening.
lessons.takeaway: Compare changes in pace, size, participation, and response.
example: Equal five-minute windows contain 10, 15, then 25 buys.
Count gains increase from +5 to +10; value and typical size also rise.
That supports accelerating sampled activity, not a predicted next candle.
evidence: Review sampled 5m activity and freshness, then compare actual windows in Inspect. Nested 5m/1h/24h totals are not separate periods.
lessons.deeper: Momentum describes sustained activity; acceleration describes a strengthening pace. Equal 180-second bars can compress the observations, but they are not mature chart structure or a mandatory interval. Compare transaction, buy and sell frequency; typical buy and sell size; unique buyers and holder growth; liquidity consumed; sell impact and dip-recovery speed; and buyer persistence. Use separate comparable periods and current coverage. Unique people, complete holder changes, and available supply may need external data. Bots, liquidity changes, and missing observations can distort the comparison.

lessons.title: Attention conversion
lessons.question: Did the story bring buyers, or only posts?
lessons.definition: The working chain is attention → unique buyers → capital traded → available supply consumed → price response.
lessons.why: More mentions can coexist with weaker buying conversion.
checks: Comparable attention and buyer observations
Trade value, seller inventory, and liquidity
Price response and missing links in the chain
lessons.healthy: Credible attention is accompanied by fresh participation and responsive demand.
lessons.dangerous: Posts accelerate while buyer arrivals and price response weaken.
lessons.mistake: Treating mention count as capital or measured conversion.
lessons.takeaway: Follow the conversion chain, not raw attention.
example: Early: 100 mentions accompany many new buyers and a strong response.
Later: 1,000 mentions accompany few new buyers and little price progress.
Investigate weaker conversion, saturation, and supply pressure.
evidence: Open source evidence, confirm the contract, then compare flow in Inspect. RSS counts do not measure total engagement or unique buyers.
lessons.deeper: Conversion efficiency is a comparison to investigate, not a Meme Fast metric. Ratios need compatible time windows, source coverage, and buyer attribution. Trading value is not total new capital, and available supply is not fully observable. Price also depends on liquidity and selling. The example supports a weakening-cycle hypothesis; it does not prove the posts caused the trades.
framework: Attention → unique buyers → capital → available supply consumed → price response.

lessons.title: Push, Hold or Fail
lessons.question: What happened after the first push?
lessons.definition: Push describes expansion; Hold describes a pause that retains the range; Fail describes loss of that range.
lessons.why: The pause helps test whether buyers are still meeting supply.
checks: Price range before and after the pause
Repeated selling and subsequent recovery
Liquidity, coverage, and alternative explanations
lessons.healthy: The range holds through repeated selling and buying resumes.
lessons.dangerous: Rebounds weaken while the range and liquidity deteriorate.
lessons.takeaway: Read the pause. Leave missing evidence unknown.
example: Price pushes higher, then pauses in a new range.
Several sells occur and price repeatedly recovers within it.
Hold is a working description; another Push still needs new evidence.
evidence: Compare candle ranges and observed swaps. Push/Hold/Fail are lesson interpretations, not automated Meme Fast classifications.
lessons.deeper: Push → Hold → Push and Push → distribution → Fail are possible paths, not rules. When history, liquidity, or wallet evidence is insufficient, use Unknown rather than forcing a state.

lessons.title: Meta saturation
lessons.question: Is the token new while its theme is already tired?
lessons.definition: Meta saturation means many similar candidates compete for attention that is no longer expanding as quickly.
lessons.why: A fresh launch can inherit an exhausted demand pool.
checks: Independent attention across the theme
Competing tokens and actual buyer arrivals
Evidence of a new catalyst rather than recycled claims
lessons.healthy: Fresh participation expands beyond existing competitors.
lessons.dangerous: New launches split the same weakening pool of attention.
lessons.mistake: Resetting expectations just because the token is new.
lessons.takeaway: Token age does not reset the meta.
example: A theme has already produced many competing tokens.
Another launches, but fresh buyer activity across the theme is fading.
Treat renewal as evidence to establish, not an automatic fresh start.
evidence: Compare exact-token source evidence across the theme, then inspect flow. Meme Fast does not certify saturation or a complete competitor universe.
lessons.deeper: Token Emergence and Meta Saturation can coexist. Reconsider the upside expectation and attention duration when the wider theme weakens; position limits belong in 303A. Many competitors alone do not prove saturation if independent attention and demand are still expanding.

lessons.title: Three basic checks
lessons.question: What is the thesis, what looks suspicious, and who is already in?
lessons.definition: These are generic, minimal entry checks for any token, whether you intend to snipe, trade PvP, or swing. They provide a quick initial assessment. Passing them does not automatically justify an entry.
lessons.why: Before shaping a trade, understand where demand could come from, how large the wave could become, and who is already positioned to sell into it.
checks: Thesis / meta / upside: what is the story, which meta does it fit, and how far could incoming demand plausibly take it from the current market cap?
Scam red flags: check bundle concentration, a working X link consistent with the exact contract, and any suspicious new or replacement CA. Check obvious sellability and liquidity problems.
Who is already in: identify notable traders, KOLs, the dev, and related wallets. Check meaningful remaining holdings and whether they are buying, holding, or selling.
lessons.healthy: The thesis is understandable, the contract links are consistent, and participant behavior supports the expected demand. Findings are brief, sourced, and explicit about unknowns.
lessons.dangerous: A familiar ticker, working X link, or known-wallet badge is treated as proof of safety or as an automatic reason to buy. Bundles, a changed CA, or existing sellers are ignored.
lessons.mistake: Turning the minimal check into a long scoring exercise, or entering simply because the token passes it.
lessons.takeaway: Use the same three checks for every entry. Keep this first pass minimal; deepen it and decide how to trade in 202A.11.
example: A new token fits an active story. State the source of possible fresh attention and a plausible upside case from its current valuation.
Compare the exact CA with project and X links, inspect bundles, and record who still holds meaningful supply. An unresolved replacement CA is Unknown, not cleared.
Summarize thesis, red flags, and participants in three short findings. Only then consider whether the expected demand supports a snipe, PvP trade, or swing.
framework: Thesis / meta / upside -> scam red flags -> who is already in.
A generic minimum for every entry; trading depth and execution belong in 202A.11.
evidence: Use listing context, sampled flow in Inspect, and followed-wallet snapshots as leads. Verify bundles, contract links, sellability, and wallet behavior externally. No badge is not proof of absence.
lessons.deeper: CA means contract address; KOL means key opinion leader. A working X link is only a consistency check, not proof that the token is legitimate. Compare exact contracts rather than names, verify any claimed replacement against primary announcements, and mark unverified information Unknown. A profitable or recognizable wallet is not automatically supportive: entry timing, position size, remaining inventory, and selling matter. A balance snapshot alone cannot establish buying or selling. Upside is a reasoned case about possible demand, not a promised target.

lessons.title: How to trade the demand wave
lessons.question: How big could the wave be, when could it arrive, and which approach can capture it?
lessons.definition: Assess the coming flow of demand first, then shape the trade around its expected size and timing. Snipe and swing are containers for capturing an early entry and selling into the rise; PvP adds competition for the same attention and capital.
lessons.why: You enter early, before the expected rise, and sell into that rise. A good story at a late price is a different opportunity. The approach must fit the demand wave rather than forcing the token into a preferred holding period.
checks: Assess the wave: use the three basic checks to identify fresh demand, plausible scale, timing, and competing tokens. For a swing, deepen all three checks before entry.
Shape the container: choose snipe, PvP rotation, or swing; define an early entry condition, exposure that fits usable liquidity, and where or when to sell into the expected rise.
Define the frame: state the required upward pressure, the time allowed for it to produce the move, and the exit when it fails, fades, or the planned rise has been captured.
lessons.healthy: Entry precedes the anticipated run. Demand and price follow-through develop inside the defined window, and exits realize gains into the rise. Exposure fits executable liquidity.
lessons.dangerous: Entry chases a wave that has already passed. The required buying fails to arrive, sellers take over, or a failed snipe is relabeled as a swing to avoid exiting.
lessons.mistake: Choosing the holding period first, treating a later recovery as proof that a failed snipe worked, or waiting indefinitely for a thesis to become demand.
lessons.takeaway: Assess the wave, build the container, enter early, and sell into the rise. If the necessary pressure fails within the defined frame and time, the trade has failed.
example: Illustrative snipe: early attention and buying are building before the run. Define a short window for upward pressure to produce the move, enter only while the early-entry condition holds, and plan to sell into the rise.

Illustrative PvP rotation: two exact-contract tokens compete for the same story. Compare fresh buyers, credible backing, remaining insider inventory, and liquidity. Stay only while the chosen wave holds; reassess a rival without chasing its completed burst.

Illustrative swing: a catalyst is expected inside 3-14 days. Deepen the thesis, supply and contract checks, and holder behavior; enter before anticipated demand, plan profit-taking into the rise, and exit if the catalyst or sustained-demand case fails.
framework: Assess demand -> choose the container -> enter early -> sell into the rise -> exit on failure.
Snipe: upward pressure must exist immediately or be building, and produce the run while you are in. Without it, within this snipe frame the trade can only go down: exit.
Frame and time define success. A later recovery outside the window cannot validate the original snipe.
evidence: Compare sampled buying, selling, absorption, and price response in Inspect; use Tweet for competing story evidence and Swing for longer-horizon leads. The scheduled sample cannot establish immediate execution timing or a complete live tape.
lessons.deeper: Snipe is a short timing approach: immediate or building buying pressure must absorb selling and produce price follow-through during the intended exposure. Set the holding window before entry; no follow-through or fading pressure means exit rather than convert it to a swing. PvP means competing for participation, often between tokens claiming the same narrative. Snipe timing can overlap with PvP; monitor current leadership, rival demand, and the cost of rotation. Swing uses the same entry checks more comprehensively: thesis, meta, comparables and catalysts over 3-14 days; liquidity and contract controls, bundles, dev sales and cheap early supply; holder composition, accumulation versus distribution, and new demand absorbing sellers. Product or ecosystem success matters only if it supports token demand. Migration may create a wave of anticipation, but technical completion alone does not create renewed buying; confirm the event and assess demand before and after. Position size, executable quotes, profit-taking and invalidation must fit the chosen window. The low and high are the intended early-entry and exit regions, not exact extrema known in advance.

principle: Snipe reads flow, not levels. Early chart history is often too short for mature technical analysis; begin with acceleration, then check the other evidence.
